title: On-die moisture sensor replaces helium leak testing of cavity packages
idea: Combine package sealing with an on-die interdigitated capacitive moisture sensor and micro-heater read out through DRAM test-mode registers: after sealing optical/mm-wave cavity memory packages, a short heat-soak and capacitance trend gives each unit's leak rate, and the sensor keeps monitoring in the field.
why: Rare-gas dependence of packaging QA: removes helium leak detection for cavity and photonic memory packages and adds field reliability telemetry at ~zero area.

title: Telephone switchboard: IGZO TFT patch panel inside the interposer
idea: An operator's switchboard re-patches calls by hand. Build ≤350 C oxide-semiconductor (IGZO) TFT pass-gate matrices into the glass or organic interposer RDL, so after test the routes between memory channels and compute PHYs can be re-patched around bad channels or re-allocated per workload.
why: Saves packages that have one bad memory channel and allows configurable memory-to-compute ratios. That is ~5-10% package yield and better use of scarce HBM.

title: Inductive broadcast stack: one coil talks to all tiers
idea: Replace through-vias with through-fields: plate 2-turn spiral coils in the RDL of thinned (<=25 um) dies stacked with adhesive; a base-die transmitter coil couples to aligned coils on every tier at once, so commands broadcast to all dies and each die replies in its own time slot.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV etch or Cu fill, ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit inductive links, made with plating and adhesive bonding only.

title: All-optical writes to magnetic memory through on-chip waveguides
idea: Eliminate electrical write drivers: deliver femtosecond laser pulses via silicon-nitride waveguides to GdFeCo-based MTJ free layers that toggle by all-optical switching; reads stay electrical via TMR.
why: Write data arriving on a photonic link is stored without O/E conversion, pushing write energy toward tens of fJ/bit and removing write-driver area.

title: Elevator destination dispatch: early row hints let DRAM pre-open
idea: Adapted from destination-dispatch elevators, where riders key in their floor in the lobby: cores send a cheap bank/row hint on a side channel tens of nanoseconds before the real request. The DRAM groups riders and opens each row once for many requests.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): ~20-40% less activation energy per useful bit and less row-hammer exposure (fact 9).

title: Predictive link coding: both ends guess, only residuals travel
idea: Ideal: send nothing because the receiver already knows. Closest achievable: run an identical tiny predictor (per-stream stride/delta or last-value) in the base die and the GPU PHY, transmit only XOR residuals with run-length coding, and resync on mismatch, like a video codec for memory traffic.
why: Fact 5: for smooth activations, KV cache and pointer-heavy data 30-60% of transferred bits are predictable, cutting link toggles and I/O energy by a similar fraction.

title: Vending machine: per-GB-hour marketplace for idle cluster DRAM
idea: Like a vending machine for memory: a software agent on each server advertises idle DRAM, and a broker rents it to memory-starved jobs as RDMA-backed far memory (swap/tier) at per-GB-hour prices, built on stock Linux and RDMA NICs. $1M covers a 4-person team for 24 months.
why: Stranded memory (often 25-40% idle) becomes usable supply with no fab; effective DRAM supply grows 10-20% per adopting cluster.

title: Passive silicon interposer becomes a trench-capacitor memory layer
idea: Exploit the scale of an otherwise idle ~2500 mm2 65 nm silicon interposer: etch deep-trench capacitors and simple access transistors into its unused area to form ~0.5-1 GB of eDRAM microns from the logic. It acts as a giant page buffer between HBM and compute.
why: Adds memory on a mature, non-EUV, U.S.-capable node (fact 4) at <1 pJ/bit and filters ~20-40% of HBM traffic.

title: Formic-acid vapor oxide reduction built into the Cu-Cu bonder
idea: Combine the solder industry's formic-acid oxide reduction with Cu-Cu micro-pillar thermocompression: dies and wafer are exposed to formic-acid vapor in nitrogen at ~200 C inside the bonder, reducing Cu2O, then pressed immediately in the same oxygen-free atmosphere, replacing argon plasma cleaning.
why: Rare-gas-free fine-pitch bonding at lower thermal budget (DRAM retention degrades with hot anneals); enables 3-10 um Cu-Cu memory stacking without argon.

title: Tree-branching TSV hierarchy sized by da Vinci's area rule
idea: Uniform TSV grids are replaced with tree-like via hierarchies: a few fat trunk TSVs at the base die branch into thinner vias at each tier, sized by the da Vinci branch rule (parent cross-section = sum of child cross-sections), which for conductors balances I^2R loss against metal volume. Upper tiers, which carry less aggregated current, get only twig-size vias and smaller keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): estimated 30-40% less TSV+keep-out area on upper dies, recovering array area and raising stack yield by cutting via count where it is not needed.

title: Wavelength-as-address: laser comb line selects the DRAM bank group
idea: Move the address decoder from nanometer on-die wiring to the rack-scale photonic spectrum: each bank group has a micro-ring receiver tuned to one comb line, so the host addresses memory by choosing which wavelength carries the request and data. One 64-line comb on a single fiber replaces 64 point-to-point links and the bank-select decode tree.
why: Attacks periphery area (fact 7) and rack-scale data movement (fact 5): fewer fibers and SerDes per GB and ~1 pJ/bit optical memory access at meter reach.

title: Wavelength is the address: passive AWG-routed photonic memory pool
idea: Ideal: addressing that costs no logic and no switching energy. Closest achievable: the host tunes a comb line whose wavelength encodes the target bank, a passive arrayed-waveguide grating steers that light to the bank's receiver, and the reply returns on the same wavelength, so bank selection needs no electronic switch or decoder tree.
why: Facts 5 and 7: removes switch, arbiter and decoder energy and area for pooled memory; latency is time of flight (~5 ns/m), keeping a rack-scale pool within DRAM-class access.

title: Mechanical vibration: GHz acoustic links replacing signal TSVs
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: ScAlN thin-film transducers on each die send 5-10 GHz bulk acoustic pulses through the stacked silicon. Each tier's receiver resonates at its own frequency, so tiers are addressed by acoustic frequency instead of by TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): signals need no TSV keep-out or bond alignment, and contactless tiers can be tested and stacked at higher yield.

title: PHY-less bonding: sense amplifiers drive logic registers directly
idea: Ideal: memory bits appear in the processor's registers with no interface at all. Closest achievable: hybrid-bond the DRAM array face-down onto logic at 1-2 um pitch so each sense-amp latch connects through its own bond to a logic-side flip-flop, deleting DQ drivers, SerDes, DLLs and the global data bus.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and periphery (fact 7): link energy drops from 3-4 pJ/bit (HBM) toward ~0.05 pJ/bit, and I/O plus global-bus periphery (~10-15% of die) disappears.

title: Tire-retreading remanufacture of DRAM dies from retired servers
idea: Harvest DRAM dies from retired server DIMMs, decapsulate them chemically, retest and bin them, then re-stack them into new CXL or inference-tier modules in U.S. remanufacturing plants, like retreading tires.
why: Raises usable supply from installed base; U.S.-located, no wafer capacity needed; low capital intensity.

title: Rectangular glass panels replace round silicon interposers
idea: Invert 'interposers are cut from round silicon wafers': build large memory-plus-logic interposers on 510x515 mm Corning glass panels with through-glass vias and 2 um redistribution lines at the Absolics plant in Georgia.
why: ~3.7x more area per substrate than a 300 mm wafer with no edge waste, low-loss glass for fast links, an all-U.S. alternative to CoWoS; target 2-3x lower interposer cost per mm2.

title: Cryogenic copper interposer at 77 K for memory packages
idea: Reverse room-temperature design: run the memory package in liquid nitrogen, where copper resistivity falls ~7x and DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude, and draw interposer lines 7x narrower or longer so more memory dies connect at the same pJ/bit.
why: Refresh nearly vanishes (fact 3) and low-RC lines enable long low-swing links (fact 5); the university fab builds the fine-line interposer, but cooling overhead (~10x at 77 K) must be paid back by data-centre-scale integration.

title: Cryotron-era cryo pods: LN2-cooled HBM with superconducting YBCO flex links
idea: Revive 1950s-80s cryogenic computing pragmatically: run memory stacks at 77 K in liquid-nitrogen pods (no helium) where DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude and copper resistance falls ~7x, and connect them to warm compute through YBCO coated-conductor flex cables.
why: Facts 3/5: refresh nearly vanishes (retention seconds to hours), wire energy and IR drop shrink, and lossless flex lets large pooled stacks sit 0.5-1 m from compute; avoids the Qatar helium chokepoint by using LN2.

title: Superconductivity: liquid-nitrogen memory pool with YBCO lossless backplane traces
idea: House pooled DRAM at 77 K where YBCO-coated tape traces carry signals with near-zero resistance and dispersion, while cold DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude so refresh nearly disappears and the leakage tail collapses.
why: Refresh tax (fact 3, 16-33% idle power) and data-movement loss (fact 5); the ~10 W/W cryocooler overhead must be beaten by refresh and I/O savings at pool scale.

title: Infrared focal-plane cubes turned sideways: memory cube edge-bonds to processor
idea: Adapted from 1990s defense IR focal-plane cube stacking: thinned DRAM dies are laminated into a cube, one side face is lapped flat, and bond pads are patterned on that face with a contact aligner. The cube stands on edge so every die's edge talks straight down to the processor.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): zero TSVs, and each die gets its own direct edge bus; tier count is limited only by die thickness, using lapping and contact lithography.

title: ADC-free time-domain readout of ferroelectric weight crossbars
idea: Eliminate the ADCs that dominate compute-in-memory: stationary NV weights in a FeFET crossbar discharge a precharged column at a rate proportional to the dot product, and a pulse-width output feeds the next layer or a time-to-digital counter.
why: Weights never move; ADCs are 50-80% of CIM energy/area, so removing them makes in-memory MACs ~5x more efficient than shipping weights at 3-4 pJ/bit.

title: Interposer fabbed as a mature-node DRAM capacity tier
idea: Combine the passive silicon interposer (2,500+ mm2 of idle silicon under every AI package) with a 2x-nm-class trench-capacitor DRAM array built into the same wafer in depreciated 300 mm lines, wired to the GPU by mm-scale interposer traces as a near tier between HBM and CXL. Arrays are tiled with stitched redundancy so a bad block is fused off instead of scrapping the interposer.
why: Capacity and capital intensity: ~10-30 GB extra per package at mature-node cost/bit with zero added footprint and ~2-4 pJ/bit access; shifts bits off scarce EUV-node wafers.

title: Display-fab chip-on-glass panels as giant memory interposers
idea: Display driver ICs are bonded to glass with anisotropic conductive film for pennies per chip. Use depreciated Gen-6/8.5 LCD lines to pattern 2 um Cu RDL on glass panels, then bond DRAM and logic chiplets with fine-pitch ACF or microbumps, making half-meter interposers that hold dozens of memory stacks.
why: Bypasses the CoWoS silicon-interposer chokepoint and its reticle limit; panel cost per mm2 ~10-20x below silicon and uses idle display capacity plus US glass makers.

title: Retired LCD fab lines reborn as panel-level memory interposer foundries
idea: Scarcity: CoWoS silicon interposer capacity is sold out. Retool depreciated Gen-6/Gen-8 TFT-LCD lines (1.5-2 um steppers, large-area sputter and CVD already installed) to pattern copper RDL interposers on 1.5 m glass panels, cutting ~100 interposers per panel instead of ~15 per 300 mm wafer.
why: Capital intensity and the HBM packaging chokepoint: fully depreciated tools and ~5-8x more interposer area per exposure, targeting 3-5x lower $/mm2 of interposer.

title: Mechanics substitution: polymer optical waveguides replace copper memory traces
idea: TRIZ #28 Mechanics substitution (replace the copper field with light): laminate siloxane polymer waveguides into ordinary PCBs on existing PCB lines, and put 28 nm VCSEL driver chips at the memory controller and on the modules, so memory channels run optically across the board. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Data movement (fact 5): longer reach without retimers lets one socket fan out to many more DIMMs, at ~3-5 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ/bit for long copper.

title: Photonic wire bonds written in place link memory and compute
idea: Box: DRAM chiplet with SiN grating couplers x standard x Ge photodiodes x free-form polymer waveguides x organic carrier x two-photon direct laser writing with closed-loop recycled solvent developer. 3D polymer waveguides are written in situ between memory and compute chiplets after placement, so no interposer and no active optical alignment are needed.
why: Water: eliminates silicon-interposer fabrication (many wet clean and plating loops) for ~10x less water per package; ~1 pJ/bit over centimetres.

title: Extruded polymer waveguides replace water-hungry memory PCB traces
idea: Box: DDR/LPDDR modules x standard x standard x 140 GHz CMOS transceivers into PTFE dielectric waveguide cables x extruded polymer x dry extrusion. Memory channels leave the motherboard entirely as 100 Gb/s mm-wave links through plastic waveguides, so boards shrink from 20+ to ~8 layers.
why: Water: every PCB layer pair adds wet etch, plating and rinse; memory-channel interconnect water falls >10x when plated layers become extruded cable; also enables memory at rack distance.

title: 3D-printed photonic wire bonds tying HBM base die to GPU
idea: Use two-photon 3D printing (like additive manufacturing at 100 nm voxels) to write freeform polymer waveguides plus printed micro-lenses between silicon-photonic ports on the HBM base die and the accelerator. Because optical loss hardly depends on length, stacks can sit centimetres away.
why: Attacks data-movement energy and shoreline limits: <1 pJ/bit links and 2-3x more stacks per accelerator because placement is not reach-limited.

title: Buffet-line broadcast: one DRAM read feeds every accelerator
idea: One buffet tray serves every diner. Likewise, a weight-streaming memory node reads each weight block once and puts it on a shared multidrop optical/SerDes broadcast bus. All N data-parallel accelerators in the pod latch it at the same moment, in a synchronized schedule.
why: Data-parallel inference replicas all read the same weights. Broadcasting cuts DRAM reads and weight capacity N-fold: 8 replicas share one copy, freeing ~7/8 of weight HBM for KV cache.

title: US Memories 2.0: binding take-or-pay buyers for a U.S. HBM-stacking plant
idea: The 1989 U.S. Memories consortium (IBM, DEC, HP, Intel and others) collapsed in January 1990 because members would not sign purchase obligations once DRAM prices fell. Re-run it for the back end only (TSV reveal, hybrid bonding, base-die attach and test of HBM/CXL modules from known-good DRAM wafers bought globally), with binding 7-year take-or-pay contracts under a price collar and a federal buyer of last resort feeding a strategic memory reserve.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital intensity: a stacking/test plant costs ~$2-4B vs $15B+ for a front-end fab and captures the HBM TSV/packaging bottleneck (fact 6); the contracts remove the price-cycle risk that killed the original.

title: Glassblown microlenses for optical vias straight through silicon
idea: Silicon is transparent at 1.3 um, so stacked dies can talk vertically by light through the bulk: reflow polymer into surface-tension microlenses (as glassblowers rely on surface tension) and use reflective silicon plasma-dispersion modulators on each tier to answer a beam sent up from the base die.
why: Eliminates TSVs entirely for data; claims sub-pJ/bit vertical links and no TSV area tax.

title: VCSEL arrays on HBM top die, fibers routed inside cold plate
idea: Combine the liquid cold plate already sitting on HBM stacks with optical I/O: bond VCSEL and photodiode arrays on the top core die (fed by TSVs from the base) and embed glass waveguide bundles inside the cold plate so light exits vertically through the plate to rack-scale memory or peer GPUs.
why: Package beachfront and pooling: adds Tb/s per stack from the top surface at ~1-2 pJ/bit over meters without consuming interposer edge.

title: Mott transition: NbO2 steep-threshold receivers enable 80 mV memory I/O swings
idea: Put NbO2 threshold-switch elements at the front end of DRAM I/O receivers; their abrupt insulator-metal transition acts as near-infinite-gain slicing so a 60-100 mV interposer swing switches cleanly, replacing 300-400 mV swings and biased sense amplifiers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): I/O CV^2 falls ~16x at 4x lower swing; HBM PHY from ~3.5 to <1 pJ/bit if sub-ns switching and endurance hold.

title: Sn: self-healing Sn-In microbumps reflowed by on-die heaters
idea: Replace SnAg microbumps in HBM stacks with Sn-In eutectic (118 C) and add polysilicon microheaters beside bump fields; when base-die link training detects rising error rates or resistance, the stack is reflowed in place during a maintenance window to heal thermo-mechanical cracks.
why: HBM field reliability and effective supply: bump cracks drive RMAs and spare provisioning; in-situ repair extends stack life and could cut replacement demand ~10%.

title: Er: erbium-amplified optical broadcast shares one weight copy
idea: Stream model weights from a single DRAM pool through an Er-doped waveguide-amplified 1-to-64 optical splitter tree, so every accelerator receives the same weight stream each step instead of each holding its own HBM copy; the amplifiers cancel the ~18 dB split loss.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: in data-parallel inference, weight replicas are often 50-80% of HBM contents; broadcast could cut total DRAM per cluster ~2-5x.

title: Passive optical splitter broadcasts one weight copy to sixteen accelerators
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Instead of every accelerator holding the full model, one memory node streams weights through a passive 1:16 optical star coupler while all 16 accelerators run the same layer in lockstep; each consumes the broadcast and keeps only activations and KV locally.
why: Duplicated weights fill much of fleet HBM; removing 15 of 16 copies raises effective capacity per purchased bit ~10x for inference, with splitters costing dollars.

title: Total internal reflection: roll-to-roll nanoimprinted polymer waveguide flex for memory optics
idea: UV-nanoimprint single-mode fluorinated-acrylate waveguides on a moving polyimide web, with tapered adiabatic couplers that mate evanescently to SiN chips; the flex carries 64+ optical lanes from memory modules to the processor package.
why: Optical memory interconnect (fact 5) at cents per lane instead of dollars per fiber-array assembly; board-scale memory pooling at ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Skyscraper sky-lobby relay dies for 32-high stacks
idea: Skyscrapers use sky lobbies so elevators run in short segments. Put a thin logic 'sky-lobby' die every 8 DRAM tiers. It re-times signals, runs local ECC and refresh control, and splits TSV chains into short, low-capacitance segments.
why: TSV load and yield get worse as stacks grow. Segmenting lets stacks reach 24-32 tiers with flat TSV energy per bit and confines faults to one segment, for ~2x capacity per package footprint.

title: Tetris: 32-byte sector fetch via burst-chop and sector-valid caches
idea: Like Tetris filling only the gaps: last-level caches track 32B sector-valid bits, and the controller issues DDR5 burst-chop or LPDDR short bursts so sparse accesses fetch half lines. Implemented in open-source controller RTL.
why: Overfetch (fact 8); 20-40% less data moved on irregular workloads.

title: Juice-concentrate links: compress in the base die before shipping
idea: Like shipping juice concentrate, a compression engine in the 12-28 nm HBM base die squeezes AI tensors 1.5-2x (exponent dedup, base-delta) before the bus; the GPU decompresses on arrival.
why: Cuts pJ per useful bit and raises effective bandwidth and capacity ~1.5x with no new memory silicon.

title: Segmentation: legacy LPDDR4 dies tiled into an HBM-emulator package
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation: instead of one tall TSV stack, tile 24-32 known-good LPDDR4/DDR4 dies from mature 1x/2x-nm DRAM lines flat on a fan-out RDL substrate from existing OSAT lines. Each die gets its own x16 channel, and a 28 nm hub die aggregates them into a 1024-bit HBM-like port. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capital and HBM tax (facts 4, 6): no TSVs, no hybrid bonders and no leading-edge DRAM wafers. Gives ~50-60% of HBM3 bandwidth at ~40% of HBM cost per GB from idle trailing capacity.

title: Fly-by-wire redundancy: erasure-code across stacks to accept defective dies
idea: Flight controls tolerate failed channels by redundancy. Stripe each cache line with a Reed-Solomon code across 8+2 stacks/channels, so stacks with dead channels or weak dies can ship and run; the controller remaps on the fly.
why: Turns part of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss into usable supply; worthwhile when yield loss exceeds the ~20% parity overhead.

title: Solution-grown YBCO superconducting interposer lines cooled by liquid nitrogen
idea: Combine coated-conductor chemistry (TFA-MOD chemical solution deposition of YBCO on solution-deposited buffers, no argon ion-beam assist or sputtering) with interposer wiring operated in LN2, so memory-to-processor transmission lines have zero DC resistance and carry low-swing signals over 10-50 cm without repeaters; no helium cryogenics.
why: Data movement and beachfront: ~0.1 pJ/bit over long reach decouples memory capacity from package edge length.

title: Synaptic pruning: over-wired glass RDL, then prune defects after test
idea: Brains overgrow synapses and then prune the unused ones. Glass interposers are built with ~2x redundant fine-pitch routes between GPU and memory sites; after assembly, built-in test finds open or shorted routes, and laser or electrical fuses prune the bad links and the unused spares.
why: Yield and cost: fine-pitch (<=2 um) RDL on glass panels is defect-limited; redundancy plus pruning could lift interposer yield from ~70% to >95% without silicon.

title: Bouligand helicoidal fiber core for warp-free organic memory substrates
idea: Mantis-shrimp clubs and beetle cuticle stack fiber plies in a slow helix, which gives isotropic stiffness and deflects cracks. Organic package cores are laid up the same way, with glass-fiber plies rotated ~15 degrees per layer instead of a 0/90 weave, giving quasi-isotropic in-plane CTE and low warpage in thin, large panels that carry many memory chiplets.
why: Lets organic substrates replace silicon interposers by staying flat enough for 10-20 um-pitch chiplet bonding; panel-level cost with no wafer-scale tools.

title: Compute embeddings from hashes instead of storing terabyte tables
idea: Recommendation embedding tables are terabytes of mostly cold rows hit by random gathers. Replace lookup with deep-hash embedding: k hashes of the ID feed a small on-accelerator MLP that synthesizes the vector, while only the hottest ~1% of IDs stay in an explicit cache.
why: Table memory falls 100-1000x and random-gather traffic disappears; trades compute and some accuracy.

title: Five-micron DRAM tiers with bitline-pitch nano-TSVs
idea: TSV diameter is set by copper fill aspect ratio (~10:1) times die thickness, so the TSV tax is really a thickness tax. Thin each DRAM wafer to 5 um on a temporary carrier and stack wafer-on-wafer, allowing 0.5 um vias at ~1 um pitch tucked into subarray gaps instead of a dedicated TSV region.
why: Removes most of HBM's ~3x area-per-bit penalty and keep-out zones while raising vertical bandwidth ~100x (fact 6).

title: Liner-free ruthenium nano-TSVs at 300 nm through 5 um dies
idea: Shrink the TSV ~20x in diameter: ruthenium needs no diffusion barrier and keeps low resistivity at small cross-sections, so dies thinned to 5 um get 300 nm Ru vias at 1 um pitch instead of 5-10 um Cu TSVs with large keep-out zones. Vias drop into the array region instead of a dedicated TSV stripe.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV plus keep-out area falls >90%, moving HBM area per bit from ~3x toward ~1.3x DDR5, and lower via capacitance trims pJ/bit.

title: Diamond via-layer lets DRAM sit directly atop hot GPU logic
idea: Scarcity: memory may not exceed 85 C yet must sit within 50 um of compute. A 20-50 um CVD-diamond interlayer (k~1,500 W/mK) with laser-drilled copper vias at 10 um pitch sits between GPU and hybrid-bonded DRAM, spreading hotspots sideways to edge cold plates before heat reaches the DRAM.
why: Data movement (fact 5): vertical DRAM-on-logic drops ~3-4 pJ/bit HBM traffic to ~0.2-0.5 pJ/bit by deleting the interposer trip; diamond makes the thermal stack survivable.

title: Flood-lit optical comb clock replaces per-channel forwarded clocks
idea: Substitute every channel's forwarded clock, DLL and PLL with one mode-locked laser that floods the backside of all chiplets at 1.3 um through the silicon; on-die photodiodes recover a common low-jitter clock so data lanes run source-synchronous with no CDR or link training.
why: Fact 7 periphery and Fact 5: removes clock lanes (~10% of pins) and DLL/PLL area and power (~15-20% of PHY power).

title: Clockless self-timed DRAM interface with no PLL or DLL
idea: Invert 'memory is synchronous': replace the DLL/PLL and forwarded clocks with delay-insensitive 1-of-4 handshake signaling between base die and host, so links idle at zero power and run as fast as local voltage and temperature allow.
why: Clock trees and DLLs burn much of DRAM I/O idle power and need retraining; self-timed links take idle I/O power toward zero and drop training latency, ~20-30% interface energy saved at low utilization.

title: Wake-once sensor: clockless delay-insensitive memory link
idea: Seismic and wildlife sensors that wake once a minute cannot afford PLL/DLL lock power. Replace forwarded clocks, DLLs and link training with a delay-insensitive 1-of-4 code: each 2-bit symbol is one transition on one of four wires plus a completion acknowledge, so energy is spent only per symbol.
why: Clocking, DLLs and idle termination are often half or more of DRAM interface power; removing them plus one transition per two bits cuts energy per access ~5-10x at typical 20-40% utilization.

title: Driverless memory die read by host-powered backscatter
idea: Eliminate the DRAM's output drivers: the processor launches a carrier on each DQ line and the memory die only toggles a tiny switch that changes the line's termination impedance (like an RFID tag), so the reflected wave carries the data; all transmit energy and big driver transistors sit on the logic die.
why: DRAM-process transistors make slow, power-hungry drivers; shifting transmit to better logic transistors at lower voltage cuts read IO energy ~30-50% and frees driver area on the DRAM die.

title: Taking out: periphery moved to a bitline-pitch bonded logic wafer
idea: TRIZ #2 Taking out the harmful part: the DRAM wafer keeps only cell mats and bitlines. Sense amps, decoders, refresh logic and the HBM PHY sit on a logic-process wafer hybrid-bonded at ~0.7 um pitch, one bond per bitline pair, so data goes from cell to PHY without crossing a slow DRAM-process wire.
why: Periphery (~49% of the die, fact 7) is recovered for cells, giving ~1.7x bits per DRAM wafer. Logic-speed sense amps and wires cut on-die movement energy ~40% and let VARY drop.

title: Interposer decoupling trenches repurposed as gigabyte-class eDRAM
idea: Ideal: the package's dead silicon stores data for free. Closest achievable: passive silicon interposers already carry deep-trench decoupling capacitors; add a 65-90 nm access transistor per trench plus simple sense periphery so the ~2,500 mm2 interposer becomes a ~0.5-1 GB eDRAM L4 directly under the HBM and GPU.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: built on depreciated 65 nm lines with no EUV (fact 4); absorbs hot traffic before it crosses into HBM (fact 5) and adds capacity per package from area already paid for.

title: Na: ion-exchanged graded-index waveguides written into soda-lime interposers
idea: Exchange Na+ ions in soda-lime or aluminosilicate glass for K+/Ag+ through a patterned mask in a molten-salt bath, writing buried graded-index optical waveguides into the glass interposer itself to route light between co-packaged optics and memory chiplets.
why: Data-movement energy and capital: optical routing at display-glass cost with no silicon-photonics fab steps; panel-scale waveguides at cents per cm2 enable multi-stack optical memory fabrics.

title: Brewed colloidal quantum-dot photodiodes coated onto memory logic die
idea: Batch-synthesize lead-sulfide or InAs quantum dots in large reactors like brewing, then spin-coat them onto a mature-node memory logic die as SWIR imagers already do. The die gets optical receivers with no III-V bonding.
why: Low-cost optical receive for memory links in non-EUV CMOS; claims a pathway to sub-pJ/bit memory optics at commodity cost.

title: Onshore HBM stacking hubs using imported known-good DRAM wafers
idea: Worsen: keep all HBM stacking and advanced packaging in one region so one disruption halts AI memory. Flip: fund U.S. packaging hubs that import known-good DRAM wafers and do TSV reveal, hybrid bonding, stacking and test domestically, since a packaging line costs ~$1-3B versus $15B+ for a fab.
why: U.S. manufacturability and supply security within ~2 years instead of 5; captures ~20-30% of HBM value-add and seeds a later fab.

title: Printing-plate kiss contact capacitive coupling for clip-on memory
idea: Place 20 um pitch electrode arrays made in 40 nm on memory and logic faces, pressed in kiss contact across 1 um of dielectric like an offset plate on a blanket. Data crosses capacitively with no metal joint, so memory clips on and off.
why: Reworkable, upgradeable memory attach with no bonding yield loss, at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit, all in non-EUV nodes.

title: Read-mostly asymmetric links: fat downstream lanes, thin upstream lane
idea: Invert 'memory links are symmetric and bidirectional': inference reads 20-100x more than it writes, so build PHYs with unidirectional memory-to-host lanes (no turnaround, simpler drivers and termination) plus a narrow write lane.
why: Removes turnaround penalty and halves transceiver complexity per lane; ~20-30% more usable bandwidth per pin and smaller PHY area.

title: Cyclos resonant clocking dropped over DVFS; memory strobes run fixed frequency
idea: Cyclos' resonant clock mesh shipped in AMD Piledriver and then vanished because on-die inductors cost area and resonance broke across wide DVFS frequency ranges. Memory interfaces run a fixed frequency per speed bin on heavily loaded clock/strobe (WCK/DQS) networks, so resonate those networks with air-core Cu inductors in the package RDL or interposer (no Co/Fe magnetics, no die area), recovering ~50-70% of their CV2 energy each cycle.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): clock/strobe toggling is ~20-30% of memory PHY power, so a claimed 10-20% total PHY energy cut using only Cu and dielectric.

title: Laser-forward-transferred copper redistribution on glass, no plating bath
idea: Box: LPDDR dies x standard x standard x fan-out RDL x glass panel x laser-induced forward transfer (LIFT) of Cu nanoparticle ink plus laser sintering. 8-15 um RDL lines are written digitally from a donor ribbon and sintered in place, replacing resist coat/develop, seed sputter, electroplating, strip and etch and the rinse after each.
why: Water: semi-additive plating lines use hundreds of litres per panel; dry digital additive writing cuts >10x and maskless writing removes photomasks.

title: C: polyethylene dielectric waveguides carry sub-THz memory traffic
idea: Drive 140-300 GHz carriers from plain CMOS transceivers into solid polyethylene/PTFE ribbon waveguides (cheap carbon-chain plastic, no lasers, no fiber alignment) between accelerator trays and memory sleds, each ribbon carrying 8-16 lanes at ~50-100 Gb/s.
why: Data-movement energy and stranded memory (fact 5): ~1 pJ/bit at 1-2 m vs ~5-10 pJ/bit for copper SerDes, making rack-level memory pooling cheap so less DRAM is provisioned per accelerator.

title: ACF failed at fine pitch; magnetically aligned iron-nickel columns fix shorts
idea: Anisotropic conductive films lost to solder at fine pitch because randomly dispersed particles bridged neighbors or missed pads. Disperse Ni-coated Fe microspheres in epoxy and cure under a vertical magnetic field so they self-assemble into isolated columns at ~10 um pitch, giving a solderless, reworkable vertical interconnect for attaching memory stacks or tiles to substrates.
why: Solder-free (no Sn, Ag, In or Au) and reworkable: a bad memory stack can be replaced instead of scrapping a $1,000+ accelerator package, attacking HBM assembly yield (fact 6).

title: Magnetic self-alignment snaps dielets into place on vibrating tables
idea: Box: DRAM dielets with patterned NiFe pads x standard x standard x self-aligned direct bonding x substrate with matching micromagnets x dry vibratory assembly. Dielets scattered on the substrate are pulled into +/-0.5 um registration by magnetic forces and then bonded, with no liquid (unlike capillary or fluidic assembly).
why: Water: dry self-assembly replaces fluidic/capillary methods and post-placement wet cleans, >10x cut; enables low-cost massive-dielet memory.

title: Array-only DRAM wafer bonded to periphery wafer at subarray IO
idea: Scarcity: the DRAM die may contain zero periphery. Build a wafer of only cell mats plus local sense amps, expose each subarray's local I/O lines and wordline-driver inputs as ~0.5 um-pitch hybrid-bond pads, and bond it face-to-face to a cheap logic wafer carrying decoders, column logic, DLL and I/O.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the die (fact 7): ~1.6-1.8x bits per DRAM wafer, and periphery moves to faster, cheaper logic with shorter on-die data paths.

title: Compiler-scheduled deterministic streaming replaces random access
idea: Transformer inference has a static access order per layer, so cache misses are a choice. The compiler emits a cycle-exact fetch schedule, and a stream engine pulls tensors from QLC NAND exactly one schedule-window ahead into a 64 MB SRAM; DRAM holds only what the compiler cannot predict.
why: Removes DRAM for static tensors (often >90% of bytes); cost per GB tracks NAND (~100x cheaper); trades generality to static-graph workloads.

title: Canal-lock stepwise charging lowers memory bus switching energy
idea: Adapted from canal locks that lift boats in stages: bus lines charge in sequence from a ladder of N tank capacitors at intermediate voltages instead of straight from VDD, so each transition dissipates ~1/N of the conventional CV^2.
why: CV^2 floor (fact 10): 4-step charging gives ~4x lower switching energy on wide slow buses, using only 180 nm switches and MIM or off-chip caps.

title: Read-as-refresh: scheduler guarantees every live row is touched
idea: Ideal: memory that never needs refreshing because it is always in use. Closest achievable: in LLM decode every weight and resident KV entry is read once per token, so the serving scheduler caps step time below 32 ms, lays tensors so each step activates every occupied row, and the base die verifies row coverage and issues no REF; sequences that go idle are evicted rather than kept.
why: Fact 3: refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power) and the 10-20% bandwidth loss go to zero for decode-dominated serving because ordinary activate-restore does the job for free.

title: Voltage-stacked HBM: dies wired in series to recycle supply current
idea: Combine voltage stacking (charge recycling) with die stacking: power a 12-high HBM from ~12 V with each die in its own 1 V domain in series, small on-die push-pull regulators balancing mismatch and level-shifting signal TSVs crossing domains. The same current is reused by every die.
why: PDN and TSV tax: supply current falls ~12x, cutting power TSV/bump count (about half of all TSVs) and IR drop; ~5-10% die area recovered and interposer PDN losses reduced.

title: Infrared optical vertical links through bondless stacks
idea: MINIFY metal in the vertical path to zero: 1.3 um infrared emitters and photodiodes send light straight through the silicon dies (silicon is transparent there), so stacked dies need no TSVs and can be separated.
why: Removes the TSV tax and makes stacks separable for repair or recycling; claims ~0.5 pJ/bit vertical links.

title: Coral-reef plating: electroless-grown pillars fuse stacked dies
idea: Stalactites and stalagmites grow until they join into a column. Align stacked dies with a small gap and flow electroless Cu/Ni bath between them. Facing pads grow until they merge into solid joints below 80 C, with no reflow or anneal.
why: Room-temperature vertical joints at <10 um pitch avoid the thermal budget and warpage, enabling many-tier stacks and denser die-to-die interfaces.

title: Coolant channels that double as liquid-core waveguides
idea: Invert 'cooling and interconnect are separate systems': microfluidic channels etched between stacked dies are filled with a high-index dielectric coolant so each channel also guides light, carrying memory-logic data while removing heat.
why: Lets memory stack directly on hot logic and adds optical bandwidth with no dedicated waveguide layers; attacks data-movement energy and HBM placement limits.

title: Light elevator: optical broadcast through windows in stacked dies
idea: Po: the chip is a window. One mask both opens a metal-free optical shaft through each die's wiring and defines a silicon ion implant forming a defect-mediated 1550 nm detector that absorbs a few percent, so one beam from the base die broadcasts clock and commands to all 16 dies in turn.
why: Deletes clock and command/address TSVs for a single mask and gives jitter-free broadcast to every die.

title: Through-silicon optical vias link stacked dies with infrared light
idea: Worsen: punch copper TSVs through every die. Flip: silicon is transparent above ~1.1 um, so bond micro-VCSEL and photodetector pairs on each die and send data vertically through the bulk silicon at 1.3 um through thinned windows, with no holes drilled at all.
why: TSV tax and yield (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area or via yield loss; short vertical optical hops at ~0.3 pJ/bit.

title: Acoustic delay lines died; AlN ultrasound carries data through stacked dies
idea: Acoustic delay-line memories died of sequential access, yet they proved GHz acoustic waves travel cleanly through solids. Put thin-film AlN bulk-acoustic transducers with Al/TiN electrodes (no Sc or Mo) on each thinned DRAM die so 5-10 GHz acoustic pulses cross the bonded silicon stack vertically, and phase a transducer array per channel to beam-steer to the target tier, giving a TSV-free, wire-free vertical data path.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): vertical data without TSVs or coils, relying on low GHz acoustic loss in Si; claimed 10-50 Gb/s per transducer cluster using Al, N, Ti and Si only.

title: Radar phased-array beams link compute boards to remote memory sleds
idea: Adapted from military AESA radar tiles: 60-140 GHz beam-steered phased arrays on memory sleds and compute boards form reconfigurable wireless links across a rack. Any accelerator can steer a beam to any memory sled without cables or connectors.
why: Disaggregation recovers stranded DRAM (often 25-50% idle per server) and removes cabling cost; target ~5 pJ/bit at 100 Gb/s per beam.

title: Phased-array radar beams to cable-free memory sleds
idea: Borrow phased-array radar beam steering. Each accelerator package and memory sled carries an in-package 140-300 GHz antenna array, forming steerable point-to-point beams across the rack. Any accelerator can attach to any memory sled with no cables or switches.
why: Enables rack-scale memory pooling that reconfigures in microseconds without optical transceivers. That could raise use of scarce DRAM 20-40%.

title: Tape-library robots shuttle preloaded CXL memory sleds between racks
idea: Treat DRAM like 1960s tape reels: a robotic library moves hot-pluggable 1-4 TB CXL memory sleds, preloaded with model weights or KV caches, to whichever rack needs them and inserts them into blind-mate CXL backplane slots in seconds.
why: Scarce-resource strategy: fleet DRAM utilization is often <50%; migrating physical capacity on minute timescales instead of over-provisioning every server could cut fleet DRAM 20-30%, and preloaded sleds avoid pushing TBs over the network.

title: Hot remote memory sleds rejecting heat through dry air coolers
idea: Box: DRAM or gain cell with retention tuned for 105 C x standard x standard x optical CXL link x air-cooled sled x standard. Memory moves out of liquid-cooled accelerator packages into separate sleds running at 45 C inlet, cooled by dry coolers with no evaporative towers.
why: Water: evaporative data-center cooling (~1.8 L/kWh) for memory heat goes to ~0, >10x cut per memory-watt; needs hot-tolerant refresh policy.

title: Free-space optical memory links through immersion coolant
idea: Po: the liquid is the wire. In immersion-cooled racks, memory sleds and accelerator boards face each other through the dielectric fluid and exchange data over arrays of collimated micro-LED and photodiode pixels (imaging links), replacing copper backplanes and cables.
why: Makes rack-scale disaggregated memory cheap (~1 pJ/bit, no connectors), recovering the 20-30% of DRAM stranded in fixed servers.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory backplane: 77 K copper for passive 2 m links
idea: Shift the temperature scale to change wire physics: memory sleds and backplane sit in LN2, where copper resistivity drops ~7x, so passive 2 m memory channels need no retimers or heavy equalization, and DRAM retention stretches to seconds so refresh nearly vanishes.
why: Rack-scale pooled-memory link energy drops ~3-5x and refresh (fact 3) nearly disappears, traded against cryocooling overhead.

title: Jacquard-woven passive optical shuffle backplane for memory pooling
idea: Weave 4,096 fibers on a loom into a fixed perfect-shuffle pattern so 64 CPUs reach 64 memory sleds all-to-all with no switches. The topology is set by the weave, like a textile pattern.
why: Pooling recovers the ~20-30% of DRAM stranded in servers, raising usable supply without new wafers; passive optics add no switch energy.

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory pods exploit 77 K copper and leakage
idea: Scarcity: no new fabs, so wring more out of existing dies. Immerse memory sleds in LN2: at 77 K copper resistance falls ~7x, so buses run 3x longer at lower swing, and access-transistor leakage collapses so refresh nearly vanishes; cryocooler cost is shared across a rack.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3, 16-33% idle power): larger pooled memory per CPU at lower pJ/bit.

title: Aircraft wireless-avionics bus inside the package cavity
idea: Airliners adopt wireless avionics intra-communication to delete harness weight. Give each chiplet a 300 GHz on-die antenna radiating into the metal-lidded package cavity, which acts as a shared multimode waveguide; frequency channels replace interposer traces, so memory chiplets can sit anywhere on a cheap organic substrate.
why: Removes dependence on silicon interposers/bridges (CoWoS chokepoint) and on beachfront geometry; any-to-any memory sharing among chiplets.

title: Copper nanowire velcro: re-mateable room-temperature interconnects
idea: MINIFY bonding heat to zero: dense interdigitated Cu nanowire arrays on both faces interlock at room temperature like nano-velcro, giving electrical contact that can be pulled apart and re-mated several times.
why: Removes solder and tin and allows rework of memory chiplets; claims ~20 um pitch with 5+ re-mating cycles.

title: Velcro: reworkable copper-nanowire hook-and-loop die stacking
idea: Forced 'velcro': dense Cu nanowire forests on both bonding faces interlock mechanically and cold-weld at room temperature at about 5 um pitch. A die that fails final test can be peeled off the HBM stack and replaced, which permanent hybrid bonds cannot allow.
why: HBM stack yield loss of 20-30%; reworkable stacks could recover most of the scrapped good dies, and room-temperature bonding avoids retention damage from heat.

title: Direct tunneling: oxide tunnel-bond hybrid bonding without metal-to-metal contact
idea: Cap both Cu bond pads with 1-1.5 nm of bond dielectric so current crosses by direct tunneling (ohmic-like at mV) plus capacitive coupling for AC; pads no longer need to expand and fuse, so dishing tolerance loosens and anneal drops below 200 C, protecting DRAM retention.
why: HBM stacking yield and pitch (fact 6): relaxes CMP/dishing specs that drive hybrid-bond yield loss, enables sub-um pitch at low thermal budget; pad tunnel resistance must stay low.

title: Holographic-memory optics revived: volume-hologram lid routes chiplet beams
idea: Revive 1960s-70s holographic page-memory optics as interconnect: memory dies emit page-wide micro-LED/VCSEL arrays upward and a volume hologram in the package lid diffracts each beam to a fixed photodiode on any of several compute chiplets, giving all-to-all fan-out without waveguide routing.
why: Facts 5/6: thousands of 5-10 Gb/s optical channels per mm^2 with no interposer wiring, ~1 pJ/bit, and broadcast fan-out for free.

title: Color-addressed banks: the wavelength is the address
idea: In DWDM networks the color routes the call. Here each DRAM bank group owns one wavelength from a host comb laser through its own microring. A request is just lighting that color on a shared bus waveguide, so routing and bank selection happen in optics with no address decode or arbitration.
why: Removes address/command wires and some of the decode and routing logic in the 49% periphery. Many banks can share one fiber, which cuts pins and pJ/bit for disaggregated memory.

title: Layer-sharded wafer-scale SRAM: weights stay put, activations flow
idea: Worsen: give every chip a full model copy in external DRAM. Flip: assign each transformer layer's weights to the SRAM of one chiplet on a wafer-scale glass panel and pass activations chip-to-chip over millimeter wires, so weights never move and no external DRAM holds them.
why: Data movement: weights are stationary and only activations move (~100x less traffic); removes DRAM for weights using mature SRAM processes.

title: Firefly-synchronized oscillator mesh replaces forwarded memory clocks
idea: Each memory channel and PHY runs a local ring oscillator weakly injection-coupled to its neighbours, so the whole package falls into phase lock the way fireflies come to flash together. That removes the global clock tree, per-byte strobes and periodic retraining.
why: Interface power and pins: strobes and clock forwarding use ~10-15% of memory interface pins and much of PHY clocking power; those pins go back to data and clocking energy falls ~30%.

title: Diffractive glass plates bake frozen model weights into optics
idea: Worsen: store weights as bits and haul them to compute billions of times. Flip: for frozen layers such as embeddings and early encoders, etch the weight matrix as phase patterns into stacked glass diffractive plates so the matrix-vector product happens as light passes through; the weights are geometry, needing no memory or data movement.
why: Removes weight storage and movement for fixed layers; glass lithography is cheap and available in the U.S. Precision and reconfigurability are the risks.

title: Xeon Phi capacity limit fixed: DRAM stacks on package underside too
idea: Knights Landing's on-package MCDRAM was abandoned largely because 16 GB was too small, a ceiling set by package beachfront beside the die. Use a glass-core substrate with 25-50 um through-glass vias to mount a second ring of memory stacks on the package underside, directly beneath the processor's I/O edge, with a board cutout and bottom cold plate, doubling the stacks within ~5 mm of the PHY.
why: Breaks the beachfront limit on stacks per accelerator: ~2x on-package capacity at the same short-reach pJ/bit, delaying the need for far memory.

title: Switch-side erasure coding replaces triple-replicated persistent memory
idea: Eliminate 3x replication traffic for durable in-memory state: the CXL switch stripes NV memory writes across 10+4 Reed-Solomon shards on different modules and computes parity in the switch, so state survives power loss and module failure.
why: Durable caches replicate over the network 3x; switch-side erasure coding needs 1.4x instead of 3x capacity and cuts durability bytes moved ~2x.

title: Sponge: porous-silicon low-k trenches under long interposer wires
idea: Like a sponge: regions of the silicon interposer under long RDL lines are electrochemically etched into porous silicon (k about 2 vs 3.9). This cuts line capacitance roughly 40%, and the CV-squared energy of cm-long chiplet links falls with it.
why: pJ/bit on 2.5D links (fact 5): roughly 30-40% lower link energy at the same swing.
